title: Private assets offer potential retirement savings boost
full_text:
Private equity could lift retirement savings more than other private assets, according to CFA Institute research that found the benefits of unlisted investments depended on asset selection, portfolio construction and retirement plan design.
The report, Private Markets in Retirement Plans: Returns, Risks, and the Importance of Plan Design, found modest allocations improved risk-adjusted performance across all five private asset classes examined: private equity, private debt, infrastructure, real estate and venture capital.
However, the findings distinguished between investments that increased average retirement balances and those that primarily reduced the variability of outcomes, highlighting different roles for private assets within superannuation portfolios.
Under its initial modelling, a target-date fund allocating 10 per cent to private equity over a 40-year accumulation period produced an average final balance 13 per cent higher than a portfolio invested solely in public equities and bonds.
Private equity delivered the highest average final balance among the portfolios examined, alongside the broadest range of final balances. Venture capital also produced a higher average balance and stronger upside outcomes than the public markets portfolio.
By comparison, allocations to private debt, infrastructure and real estate produced lower average final balances than the baseline portfolio. Their improved risk-adjusted performance reflected reduced volatility in accumulation outcomes.
The highest average annual Sharpe ratios, the study’s measure of risk-adjusted performance, were observed in portfolios allocating to private equity or venture capital.
CFA Institute head of advocacy and policy research, Olivier Fines, said the assessment needed to extend beyond headline returns.
“The relevant test is whether a private market allocation adds value after fees and within the liquidity, valuation, and governance constraints of a defined contribution plan. Our analysis shows that the answer depends on the asset class and the design of the plan,” Fines said.
The research modelled regular contributions into target-date funds, which adjust their investment mix as members approach retirement, to compare portfolios with and without private market allocations.
Its initial analysis maintained a 10 per cent allocation to a single private asset class throughout accumulation, while testing changes to allocation sizes, investment horizons and the transition from equities to bonds.
Australia’s compulsory superannuation system was among the retirement markets considered, with the release noting that Australian superannuation assets reached $4.77 trillion in the June 2026 quarter.
The report identified Australia as a market where large funds already used private investments as established components of long-term portfolios, placing greater emphasis on the conditions under which those assets were managed.
CFA Society Australia chief executive Lisa Carroll said domestic funds had substantial experience investing across unlisted markets.
“Large superannuation funds already treat unlisted infrastructure, property, private equity, and private credit as established building blocks for long-horizon portfolios, with Australian policy focused on valuation, liquidity, and governance,” Carroll said.
“Importantly, this new report finds that retirement funds with allocations to private equity or venture capital show a higher average end accumulation value and stronger upside performance than those only investing in public equities and bonds.”
The report pointed to APRA’s December 2024 thematic review of unlisted asset valuation and liquidity risk management, highlighting expectations around timely and reliable valuations, board oversight, conflict management, revaluation triggers and credible liquidity frameworks.
It also identified the importance of valuations in a unit-priced superannuation system, where the value assigned to unlisted investments affects fairness between members entering and exiting funds.
Combining different private assets changed the modelled results, reinforcing the importance of assessing their contribution within a broader portfolio.
Pairing venture capital with private debt, infrastructure or real estate reduced volatility and modestly improved risk-adjusted performance compared with allocating the private market component solely to venture capital.
Adding those defensive assets alongside private equity also reduced the variability of final balances, but lowered risk-adjusted performance compared with the private-equity-only allocation.
The findings suggested that funds seeking higher average balances could assess private equity and venture capital differently from funds prioritising more stable accumulation outcomes.
“The key message from the report is that private market inclusion in accumulation plans should be carefully considered and calibrated into retirement portfolios; it should account for portfolio construction considerations and associated costs, liquidity and fee constraints, retirement outcomes, and fiduciary governance,” Carroll said.
The research also found that retirement plan design could influence outcomes as much as, or more than, the decision to include private assets.
In particular, the accumulation period and the timing of the transition from equities to bonds affected final balances, with the initial modelling shifting portfolios towards bonds over the final 10 years before retirement.
The report concluded that private market allocations needed to be assessed within the overall investment strategy, including liquidity needs, operational capacity and members’ tolerance for risk.
Its results were based on simulations and assumptions about contributions and portfolio construction, with consistent contributions over long periods remaining central to retirement adequacy.
“Ultimately, contribution levels and the time horizon over which cash flows are compounded are the most important aspects of securing adequate retirement income,” Carroll said.
